title: 4 signs a rescue video is staged

scenes.headline: No real rescue group named
scenes.body: Genuine rescues name an organisation you can look up.

scenes.headline: Filming starts before helping
scenes.body: Several camera angles and heavy edits usually mean the 'danger' was planned.

scenes.headline: Same animal, same setting, again
scenes.body: Repeat 'rescues' on one account are a red flag.

scenes.headline: It asks you for money
scenes.body: 21% of the fake-rescue posts in one study asked viewers to donate.

scenes.label: views on 1,022 fake-rescue links
scenes.body: Found in six weeks across five platforms.

caption:
A fake rescue is animal abuse with a happy ending edited on.

Cats were the most-featured animals (42%), followed by primates, dogs, snakes and turtles. Don't share, comment on or rewatch them — engagement is what pays.

Source: Social Media Animal Cruelty Coalition, 'Spot the Scam' (2024), via World Animal Protection. Photos/video: Wikimedia Commons (credits on screen).
notes: AVOID format: anti-pattern explainer only — we never post rescue narratives. Uses calm wild macaque photos (labelled 'not a rescue'), no staged footage; teaches the SMACC red flags.
